newsitem.title: UK: GEC shares slip as merger-deal hopes dashed.
newsitem.headline: GEC shares slip as merger-deal hopes dashed.

text.p: General Electric Co Plc saw its share price slide on Tuesday as market hopes for a defence merger deal were dashed after the engineering giant unveiled its strategic blueprint.
Despite flagging the possible flotation of GEC-Alsthom, the power-to-rail division, GEC shares were down 20p at 357-1/2 by 1250 GMT.

Recent sessions saw a storm of speculation about the possibility of GEC announcing a defence deal with either Finmeccanica SpA of Italy or British Aerospace Plc . Both failed to materialise, leading to a kneejerk fallback in GEC shares, analysts said.
"After all the speculation about defence deals, nothing was announced," said Mike Styles, analyst at Credit Lyonnais Laing.

Reflecting on GEC's recent 10-percent share price gain on the speculation, another analyst said: "Sometimes it is better to travel than to arrive. Actually I thought GEC revealed more than I'd been expecting. But others had obviously expected concrete deals and did not get them."
Styles said the fall in the share price was inevitable after the build-up of expectations, but he pointed to the positive news that had come from the group.

"They have said they will come to decision (on whether to demerge or float) GEC-Alsthom within three months. There will be some acquisitions on the GEC-Marconi (defence business) side and (managing director George) Simpson has talked about possibly returning cash to shareholders."
But Andy Crispin, analyst at SocGen, was more downbeat. He said the timescale to deliver value to shareholders was three to four years -- too long a timeframe to buy the shares now.
Commenting on Simpson's plans to grow GEC-Marconi through acquisitions, Crispin said the current valuation of the stock market would make it difficult for GEC to find suitable deals.
"A deal could take as long as 18 months," he said.

He said GEC-Alsthom's future was still subject to discussions, and was similarly cautious about how long it would take to develop the business of the telecoms joint venture GPT, which GEC is committed to.

But Styles said he was reasonably optimistic on Simpson's ability to deliver. Another industry analyst said: "There's a lot to be excited about", adding that the share price fall had to be taken in context. "The shares were around 340 pence only a short time ago. So we shouldn't get too excited by the fall."

On the possible proceeds from the flotation of GEC-Alsthom, analysts said it could raise between three and 3-1/2 billion pounds in total, with GEC taking a half-share in that and its partner Alcatel Alsthom taking the other half.
